method: OPEN AND QUOTED from French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes' (published 30 April 2023). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10148979).

claims.claim: **Definitions:** eosinophilia is 0.5-1.5 per nL; hypereosinophilia (HE) is above 1.5 per nL and/or tissue eosinophilia. HES is diagnosed as soon as HE is judged to cause organ dysfunction, whatever the cause.
claims.source_text: this classification distinguishes blood eosinophilia (between 0.5 and 1.5 × 109/L eosinophils), HE (blood eosinophilia > 1.5 × 109/L and/or tissue eosinophilia) … the diagnosis of HES is made as soon as blood and/or tissue HE is found to be the cause of clinical organ dysfunction (regardless of the underlying mechanism/etiology of HE)
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The eosinophil count does not track severity**; organ damage depends on tissue infiltration and eosinophil activation. With urgent, life-threatening disease, a 1-month wait before diagnosing HES is no longer required.
claims.source_text: Generally, there is no correlation between the level of blood HE and the severity of clinical manifestations (which is more closely related to the extent of eosinophilic tissue infiltration and the degree of eosinophil activation within tissues). … a minimal delay of 1 month is no longer required before the diagnosis of HES can be retained.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Emergencies:** eosinophilic myocarditis, intracardiac thrombus with embolism, severe asthma or hypoxic lung disease, strokes and arterial or venous thrombosis. A very high count alone (for example above 10 per nL) without clinical involvement is not an emergency.
claims.source_text: These mainly include cardiac manifestations (e.g., eosinophilic myocarditis, intracavitary thrombosis with peripheral or cerebral embolic events, coronary artery spasm, acute heart failure), respiratory disorders (severe acute asthma or hypoxic lung disease), central nervous system manifestations (typically strokes of bilateral watershed distribution) and thrombotic (either arterial or venous) events … Contrariwise, in the absence of overt clinical manifestations, very high eosinophil counts (e.g., > 10 × 109/L) are not per se an indication for emergency initiation of treatment.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The GP starts the work-up** (history, examination, first-line tests for drug and parasitic causes), but must refer to an organ specialist without delay for unusual symptoms or suspected cardiac, respiratory, thrombotic or neurological disease.
claims.source_text: A general practitioner or pediatrician who will conduct a history-taking interview and perform a comprehensive physical examination (possibly supplemented by basic first-line investigations) to screen for the most common causes of HE (drug-related or parasitic infection, as detailed in "Pharmacological treatments" section) and potential related complications. This initial workup must not delay the referral to an organ specialist physician if there are any unusual symptoms or if serious (cardiac, respiratory, thrombotic, neurological) disease is suspected.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For recent-onset HE above 1.5 per nL, look first for drugs and parasites.** Drug-induced HE usually appears 2-8 weeks after starting the drug; common culprits include NSAIDs, antiepileptics, antibiotics, sulfonamides and allopurinol. Stop the suspect drug where possible.
claims.source_text: In the presence of recent onset HE > 1.5 × 109/L: etiologic investigations should focus on drugs and parasites … The duration of HE (and the temporal relationship between its onset and the initiation of a drug, typically 2-8 weeks) is an important consideration. Likewise, the history of previous CBC can be instructive. The main drug classes that are routinely implicated in HE are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antiepileptic drugs, antibiotics, sulfonamides and allopurinol … Whenever in doubt (and whenever possible), an attempt to discontinue the potential culprit drug/product should be performed.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspect a clonal (myeloid) cause** with hepato- or splenomegaly, cytopenia, thrombocytosis, polycythaemia, monocytosis, basophilia, raised vitamin B12 or tryptase, or eosinophils that do not normalise on steroids. Endomyocardial fibrosis, border-zone strokes and mucosal ulcers point strongly to FIP1L1::PDGFRA disease, which is mainly seen in men.
claims.source_text: Overall, some clinical (hepatomegaly, splenomegaly) and/or laboratory (cytopenia, thrombocytosis, polycythemia, monocytosis, basophilia, elevated serum vitamin B12 and/or tryptase) characteristics and/or the lack of normalization of absolute eosinophil count under treatment with systemic corticosteroids are suggestive of clonal HE. … some clinical manifestations (endomyocardial fibrosis, bilateral border zone strokes, lymphomatoid papulosis, and mucosal ulcerations) are highly suggestive of F/P + chronic eosinophilic leukemia, the latter having a very clear male predominance
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **First test for clonal HE: FIP1L1::PDGFRA by RT-PCR or RQ-PCR on peripheral blood.** If blood molecular tests are negative, do a bone marrow aspirate with karyotype and FISH for ABL1, PDGFRB, PDGFRA and FGFR1 rearrangements.
claims.source_text: The first test to perform is the search for FIP1L1::PDGFRA (F/P) by nested reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) or real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RQ-PCR) in peripheral blood … If the molecular workup on peripheral blood is negative, a bone marrow aspiration with conventional karyotyping and FISH (to detect translocations involving ABL1, PDGFRB, PDGFRA or FGFR1) is recommended.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Screen every patient for cardiac involvement promptly**, because it can be silent early and late diagnosis carries a poor prognosis. In FIP1L1::PDGFRA disease, cardiac and brain MRI are suggested first-line even when troponin, BNP and echo are normal.
claims.source_text: cardiac involvement should be routinely and promptly screened for (even in children). … it seems appropriate to recommend cardiac and cerebral MRI as first-line examinations (even in asymptomatic patients, and/or if first-line tests, such as troponin/BNP and TTE, are normal).
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not let the work-up delay treatment of life- or organ-threatening HES:** prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, preceded by IV methylprednisolone 15 mg/kg for 1-3 days depending on the picture, together with antiparasitic treatment.
claims.source_text: In these emergency situations, while the etiologic workup is also urgent, it should never delay the initiation of treatment. … is based on corticosteroid therapy (prednisone: 1 mg/kg/day, preceded by intravenous pulses of methylprednisolone 15 mg/kg for 1-3 days, depending on the clinical picture), in combination with antiparasitic treatment
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Give ivermectin 200 µg/kg before steroids** (unless contraindicated) to prevent severe strongyloidiasis.
claims.source_text: Preemptive treatment with ivermectin (200 µg/kg on an empty stomach) is recommended (in the absence of contraindications) for prophylaxis of severe strongyloidiasis.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Steroid-resistant HES** means no clinical or laboratory response after 3 days of corticosteroids and should prompt a search for other causes, including clonal disease.
claims.source_text: In case of steroid-resistant HES (defined as the absence of clinical and laboratory response after 3 days of corticosteroid therapy), the main etiologies to be investigated are as follow:
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat every patient, with or without symptoms, and start promptly**: persistent HE risks irreversible (especially cardiac) damage and leukaemic transformation, and delay raises relapse risk after later stopping.
claims.source_text: it is recommended that treatment be initiated in any patient with F/P + chronic eosinophilic leukemia, symptomatic or not []. In addition, as the time to initiation of treatment appears to be correlated with the risk of relapse following attempts to discontinue treatment, it is recommended that treatment be initiated promptly once a diagnosis of F/P + chronic eosinophilic leukemia has been made
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **First line is imatinib 100 mg daily**, which gave molecular remission in 100% of the authors' patients. In a severe, suggestive presentation it can be started before the PCR result. Male and female contraception is required.
claims.source_text: First-line treatment consists of imatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, which achieves laboratory and molecular remission in 100% of cases in our experience. A dose of 100 mg daily is sufficient to achieve a complete response, while improving tolerability … The introduction of imatinib may be recommended even before the result of the FIP1L1::PDGFRA test when the patient's condition is severe, and the clinical and laboratory findings are suggestive of such diagnosis. It is important to note that treatment with imatinib requires the use of both male and female contraception.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **With cardiac involvement, check troponin 48 h after starting imatinib** (in hospital if heart disease is severe), and give a short steroid course (for example 1 mg/kg/day for 5-7 days) if troponin rises.
claims.source_text: This warrants laboratory monitoring of troponin 48 h after initiation of treatment (which should be done in hospital in case of severe eosinophilic heart disease), and the prescription of a short course of corticosteroids if troponin increases during imatinib treatment (e.g., 1 mg/kg/day corticosteroids for 5-7 days).
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If imatinib seems to fail, check adherence and absorption first, then reconsider the diagnosis.** Rare resistance mutations (T674I, D842V) may respond to dasatinib or nilotinib.
claims.source_text: Non-compliance to treatment (or a pharmacokinetic issue related to imatinib malabsorption). … Second-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as dasatinib and nilotinib, have been shown to be effective in vitro on both wild-type and mutated tyrosine kinases, and treatment success has been described with both compounds in this situation
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Duration:** imatinib can continue long term; a stop can be tried case by case after at least 5 years in prolonged molecular remission (about 40% stay in remission). Molecular monitoring is mandatory: every 3 months in year one, then every 6 months.
claims.source_text: suggests that ≈ 40% of patients can maintain sustained molecular remission after initial discontinuation of imatinib … Treatment with imatinib 100 mg/day can be administered on a long-term basis, but cessation can also be attempted on a case-by-case basis after a minimum of 5 years of treatment in patients in prolonged molecular remission. Regular molecular follow-up (even in the absence of recurrence of eosinophilia) is mandatory (e.g., every 3 months in the first year and every 6 months thereafter).
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other PDGFRA fusions** (partners such as BCR, ETV6, KIF5B) respond, like FIP1L1::PDGFRA, to low-dose imatinib 100 mg daily.
claims.source_text: Clonal forms of HES involving PDGFRA and a partner gene (such as BCR, ETV6, KIF5B, etc.) other than FIP1L1 are possible. Although exceedingly rare, and by analogy with F/P + chronic eosinophilic leukemia, they are also particularly sensitive to low dose imatinib (i.e., 100 mg daily)
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **PDGFRB rearrangements** (for example ETV6::PDGFRB, which can look like CMML) usually respond to imatinib but at a higher starting dose of 400 mg daily, which may be reduced carefully to 100 mg once molecular remission is reached.
claims.source_text: Rearrangements involving PDGFRB and other partners (about 30 to date) have been reported, including ETV6::PDGFRB, which may also be responsible for a chronic myelomonocytic leukemia phenotype with HE due to t(5;12)(q32;p13). These cases are generally responsive to imatinib (MA), but initially at higher doses (400 mg daily) than those used to treat F/P + chronic eosinophilic leukemia [, ]. These dosages generally result in prolonged molecular remission with continued treatment. Once molecular remission is achieved, careful reduction of the doses to 100 mg imatinib may be suggested, subject to regular molecular monitoring.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **FGFR1, JAK2 and FLT3 rearrangements are aggressive and imatinib-resistant;** they need specialist or trial-based targeted therapy and consideration of allogeneic transplant.
claims.source_text: JAK2 rearrangements (including PCM1::JAK2 due to t(8;9)(p22;p24) and BCR::JAK2 due to t(9;22)(p24;q11)) are sensitive to JAK2 inhibitors, including ruxolitinib (off label). However, response to treatment may be transient and this therapeutic approach is usually a bridge to allogeneic bone marrow transplantation, which should be considered (depending on the patients' age and comorbidities) … FGFR1 rearrangements, including FGFR1::ZMYM2 due to t(8;13)(p11;q12), are associated with aggressive clinical phenotypes with, in the absence of treatment, constant and rapid progression (in one to two years) towards a high-grade hematological malignancy (acute myeloid leukemia, lymphoblastic lymphoma) resistant to standard TKIs (including ponatinib) … Patients with FLT3 rearrangements generally have an aggressive phenotype resistant to the main TKI.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Corticosteroids are first line** and usually work quickly. Prefer local steroids where possible; when systemic treatment is needed use prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day, then taper to the lowest effective dose. In chronic disease about 12 months of treatment is advised before trying to stop.
claims.source_text: Corticosteroid therapy is generally the first-line treatment for idiopathic HES, and rapid response (complete or partial) is the norm. … The loading dose (0.5-1 mg/kg/day prednisone (off-label)), possibly preceded by pulses of methylprednisolone (15 mg/kg/day for 1-3 days) in case of organ- or life-threatening manifestations, should be tailored to the severity of symptoms before gradual tapering. Overall, the minimum effective dose should be used, and weaning should always be discussed: in acute forms, cessation of corticosteroid therapy may be attempted after a few weeks of treatment; in the case of chronic disease, a treatment period of approximately 12 months seems advisable before considering cessation.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mepolizumab 300 mg subcutaneously monthly is the recommended first steroid-sparing drug** for chronic steroid-dependent idiopathic HES, or relapsing HES with at least 3 steroid-requiring flares a year. It has no role as first-line therapy.
claims.source_text: we currently recommend mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneous monthly) as the first-line steroid-sparing agent. … Chronic AND idiopathic AND oral-corticosteroid-dependent HES (meaning that the efficacy of oral corticosteroids has previously been established, and that an attempt to withdraw oral corticosteroids has been followed by both a clinical AND a hematological relapse) Relapsing (either single-organ OR systemic) HES with at least 3 yearly flares requiring short courses of oral costicosteroids. … there is to date no rationale for the prescription of mepolizumab either as first-line therapy
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After mepolizumab failure:** pegylated interferon alfa-2a (start 45 µg weekly) or hydroxycarbamide (start 1 g/day, up to 2 g/day). Empirical imatinib 400 mg/day may be tried when myeloid features are present, stopping if there is no response at 1 month.
claims.source_text: It is therefore standard practice to start with the lowest possible dosage (e.g., 45 µg pegylated interferon alfa-2a weekly by subcutaneous injection) and to increase it gradually monthly if necessary, depending on tolerability. … In practice, it is usually started at a low dosage (1 g/day in a single dose) and then increased if necessary (up to 2 g/day in a single dose) depending on effectiveness and tolerability … imatinib (400 mg/day) may also be used empirically (and off label) in patients with laboratory and clinical findings suggestive of underlying myeloid malignancies (although by definition, idiopathic HES does not show the cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities characteristic of clonal HES) e.g. splenomegaly, elevated vitamin B12 or tryptase, presence of other CBC abnormalities, nonresponse to corticosteroid therapy (or corticosteroid dependence on more than 10 mg/day prednisone) []. In the absence of response at 1 month after initiation of imatinib, the latter should be discontinued and replaced by another steroid-sparing drug.
claims.locator: French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes', published 30 April 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10148979/, retrieved 2026-09-23
